parsed.title: End-to-End Learning for Autonomous Driving: Approaches and Simulation Platforms
outline: Introduction to end-to-end learning in autonomous driving
Comparison of CNN and RNN architectures
Simulation and mid-level representations in training
parsed.markdown:
End-to-end learning approaches for autonomous driving involve training models that directly map sensory inputs to control commands. Bojarski et al. [1] present a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the entire processing pipeline to steer an automobile, generating steering commands from a single front-facing center camera image. Dosovitskiy et al. [2] introduce CARLA, an open urban driving simulator used to study multiple autonomous driving approaches including end-to-end imitation learning, supporting training, prototyping, and validation of models involving perception and control.

Bansal et al. [3] propose ChauffeurNet, a recurrent neural network (RNN) that takes mid-level input representations and outputs driving trajectories for control. ChauffeurNet includes components such as FeatureNet and AgentRNN, with recurrent feedback mechanisms between iterations to refine predictions. This contrasts with the CNN approach of Bojarski et al. [1], which directly generates steering commands from raw camera images.

Both ChauffeurNet [3] and CARLA [2] emphasize the use of mid-level representations and simulation environments to facilitate autonomous driving training and testing. ChauffeurNet enables training on real or simulated data and supports closed-loop simulation testing before deployment. CARLA provides a flexible platform for specifying sensor suites and environmental conditions, allowing controlled scenario evaluation and supporting development and validation of autonomous urban driving systems.

Despite these advances, there is a lack of direct empirical comparison between the end-to-end CNN approach [1] and the mid-level input/output RNN approach [3] under the same conditions or datasets. This gap highlights an opportunity for future research to evaluate the relative performance and trade-offs of these fundamentally different architectures in autonomous driving tasks.
